new_statements.rule_in_words: Katuic words (Ta'oiq/tth included) are at most disyllabic iambs: an optional reduced presyllable plus a main syllable; the main, word-final syllable carries the prominence and the presyllable is unstressed; monosyllables are bare main syllables. Hence stress is word-final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; native words are maximally disyllabic so the question does not arise.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The second quoted sentence is framed for the Proto-Katuic template (after Sidwell 2005) which the author treats as inherited by the modern languages; the first sentence is his own synchronic generalisation over all Katuic languages. Van der Haak 1993 adds only that Ta'uaih Ca presyllables have a slightly longer vowel than CaC presyllables and that checked, -s and -h syllables have relatively high pitch in isolation (p.260-261), with no stress rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Family-level typological statement (all Katuic; paper's ISO list includes tth and it draws on the author's Ta'oiq field data), domain = phonological/prosodic word; nothing on phrase-level prominence or citation forms. No Ta'oih-specific published sentence on stress was found: the only dedicated phonology (van der Haak 1993) is silent but analyses words as presyllable + main syllable with a quality-neutral presyllable vowel, and L-Thongkum 2002 writes a stress mark before the final syllable of Ta Oi' forms; both are consistent with the iambic/final reading.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog uppe1406 / ISO tth covers two Lao varieties that the recent literature separates: (a) Ta'uaih = Ta'uas, 'High Ta-oih proper' (van der Haak 1993, speaker from Ban Tung Wiih, Muang Ta'oi, Salavan; no register contrast; Diffloth 1989 n.2), and (b) Ta'oiq, also called Ong / Ir / Katang(-Ta'oih), with a tense-marked register (Gehrmann & Conver 2015: lvi; Gehrmann 2018 labels his data 'Ta'oiq [tth]'; note ISO oog 'Ong' also exists). The quoted statement is family-level (all Katuic) by an author whose own field data are Ta'oiq. L-Thongkum's 'Ta Oi'' of Tha Taeng is equated by Glottolog with Lower Ta'oih (lowe1412? tto) and her 'Kantu' with tth. Vietnamese-language works on 'tieng Ta Oi' (A Luoi, Thua Thien-Hue; e.g. Tran 2013, Nguyen Van Loi et al. 1986) are, per Gehrmann & Conver 2015, linguistically Pacoh-group (paco1243) rather than the Lao Ta'oi branch, so they should not be used for tth without checking.

sources.note: p.133: Katuic languages (ISO list on p.132 explicitly includes tth) have 'prosodic words of a maximally disyllabic, iambic template'; the presyllable is 'always unstressed', the final/main syllable 'always prosodically prominent' (stated for the Proto-Katuic word template after Sidwell 2005 and carried through the modern languages); abstract p.132 'the unstressed, penultimate syllable (presyllable)'. Ta'oiq-specific remarks concern presyllable shape only (stop+liquid presyllables realised [Crə], pp.138-139), not stress.

sources.citation: van der Haak, Feikje. 1993. Ta'uaih phonology and orthography: a preliminary statement. Mon-Khmer Studies 22: 257-264.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a Harvard login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: No explicit stress statement anywhere in the 8 pages. Words are analysed as an optional presyllable (Ca with slightly longer vowel, or CaC with -r/-l/-w/-N coda; presyllable vowel /a/ 'non-contrastive in its quality', p.261) plus a main syllable; p.260 note 6: syllables closed by stops, post-glottalised finals, /s/ or /h/ 'have a relative high pitch when spoken in isolation'. Speaker from Ban Tung Wiih, Muang Ta'oi, Salavan (Ta'uaih = 'High Ta-oih' proper).

sources.citation: Gehrmann, Ryan & Johanna Conver. 2015. Katuic phonological features. Mon-Khmer Studies 44: lv-lxvii (Notes, Reviews, Data-Papers).
sources.note: Comparative survey of Katuic onsets, codas, vowels/registers and minor syllables; no statement on stress placement. Useful identity information p.lvi: Ta'oi sub-group = Ta'oiq (Ong/Ir/Katang, tense-marked register) and Ta'uas (= Ta'uaih/Ta'oih, no register); Vietnamese 'Ta'oih' belongs with Pacoh. Cites unpublished Conver, Conver & Schmutz 2014 'Ta'oiq phoneme inventory and word list'.

sources.citation: Schmutz, Jonathan. 2013. The Ta'oi language and people. Mon-Khmer Studies 42: i-xiii.
sources.note: Literature/ethnonym review only; states that linguistic publications on Ta'oi are limited to Watson 1969, van der Haak 1993 and Solntseva 1996 plus wordlists (Nguyen Van Loi et al. 1986, Theraphan 2001, Ferlus n.d., Miller 1988). Nothing on stress.

sources.note: No prose statement on stress; comparative tables transcribe Ta Oi' (Tha Taeng; Glottolog equates this variety with Lower Ta'oih tto) and 'Katu' disyllables with a stress mark before the final syllable (e.g. Ta Oi' ta'kaal 'eight', ka'saj), i.e. implicit final-syllable stress.

sources.citation: Diffloth, Gerard. 1989. Proto-Austroasiatic creaky voice. Mon-Khmer Studies 15: 139-154.
sources.note: Discusses creaky vs plain rimes in Talan and Ong (Katang-Ta'oih area, Muang Ta-oy, Saravan); nothing on word stress. Note 2: speakers distinguish themselves from the /taʔuas/, 'the proper Ta-oih or High Ta-oih'.
